# Getting started on the cluster

Getting from zero to a shell prompt: what the machine is, how to get an account, and how to log in.

## What a cluster is {#sec-cluster}

### Mental model

MedicineBow is not one big computer. It is a few hundred ordinary Linux servers ("nodes")
wired together, all mounting the same shared filesystems, all managed by a program that
decides whose job runs where and when. That program is the **scheduler** (here,
[Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/)). Learning the cluster is mostly learning to work
*with* the scheduler.

### Login nodes vs. compute nodes

There are two kinds of machines, and confusing them is the most common beginner mistake.

**Login nodes** (`mblog1`, `mblog2`) are the front door. When you `ssh` in or open a
terminal in the web portal, you land here. They are shared by everyone at once — dozens of
people editing files, submitting jobs, and moving data. Use them for lightweight work:
editing scripts, managing files, compiling small things, submitting and checking jobs.

**Compute nodes** are where computation happens. You never SSH to them directly; you ask
the scheduler for one (or many), and it gives you exclusive, accounted-for access for a
bounded time. The default `mb` nodes have **96 CPU cores and ~1 TB of RAM each**, and the
GPU nodes carry up to **8 NVIDIA H100s**.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-nodes
%%| fig-cap: "You reach a shared login node from your laptop; the scheduler runs your jobs on dedicated compute nodes. All nodes see the same filesystems."
flowchart LR
    U["Your laptop"] -->|"ssh / web portal"| L
    subgraph MB ["MedicineBow"]
        L["Login nodes<br/>mblog1 / mblog2<br/>shared, lightweight only"]
        S{{"Slurm scheduler"}}
        L -->|"sbatch / salloc"| S
        S --> C1["Compute node"]
        S --> C2["Compute node"]
        S --> C3["GPU node"]
    end
    FS[("Shared filesystems<br/>home, project, scratch")]
    L --- FS
    C1 --- FS
    C3 --- FS
    style MB fill:#f3eefb,stroke:#7a4fb5,color:#3a2a5a
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Don't compute on login nodes
A heavy job on `mblog1`/`mblog2` — a big simulation, a data-crunching Python script, a
multi-hour build — slows the machine for everyone logging in. ARCC monitors this and kills
runaway login-node processes (and emails you).

Rule of thumb: anything that takes more than a couple of minutes, or uses more than a core
or two, belongs in a Slurm job or an interactive session. See @sec-why-scheduler.
:::

### Why share a machine at all?

If everyone had their own dedicated server, most servers would sit idle while a few people
occasionally needed far more than one server could give. Pooling the hardware and
scheduling access means:

- When you need 50 nodes for an ensemble, you can have them (briefly).
- When you need nothing, someone else uses the hardware you're not using.
- A fair-share accounting system stops any one person from hogging everything.

In exchange, you sometimes **wait in line** and you have to **describe your work up front**
(how many cores, how much memory, how long). Most of this book is about making those two
things painless.

### What MedicineBow is, concretely

MedicineBow is a RHEL 9 Linux cluster. Its hardware is a mix of:

- **General CPU nodes** (the `mb` partition): 25 nodes, 96 cores and ~1 TB RAM each.
- **GPU nodes**: H100, L40S, A30, A6000, and R6000 flavors — for ML, PINNs, and anything
  CUDA.
- **Absorbed older clusters**: the retired *Teton*, *Beartooth*, and *WildIris* clusters
  now live on as large partitions inside MedicineBow. Teton alone is ~250 nodes.
- **Investor ("condo") nodes**: hardware bought by specific research groups, which others
  can borrow when it's idle — but the owner can reclaim it and bump your job (see
  @sec-preemption).

The partition chapter (@sec-partitions) covers which
hardware to ask for, and the queue-times chapter (@sec-queue-times) covers which choices
leave you waiting versus running now.

## Getting an account {#sec-account}

### How to request an account

Access to MedicineBow for ASCEND/ARID performers is coordinated through the program. To
request an account, email **Virginia Iglesias** (<virginia@innosphere.org>) and mention that
you're an ASCEND/ARID performer who needs MedicineBow access. She'll arrange for you to be
added to the project.

Accounts are tied to a project — for this work that's `cowy-firesurro` (the project this
guide was written under), which is also the name you type into **every job** you run
(@sec-anatomy).

### UW accounts vs. ARCC-Only accounts

ASCEND spans UW, CSU, CU Boulder, Mines, NCAR, and NEON, so this distinction affects
collaborators:

| | Full UW account | ARCC-Only account |
|---|---|---|
| Who | UW-affiliated people | External collaborators without a UW identity |
| HPC (MedicineBow) | ✅ | ✅ |
| GitLab | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Globus data transfer** | ✅ | ❌ **cannot use Globus** |
| Other UW services | ✅ | ❌ |

::: {.callout-warning}
## ARCC-Only accounts and Globus
External collaborators on ARCC-Only accounts **cannot use Globus**, the recommended way to
move large datasets (@sec-moving-data). They'll need a *guest collection* set up for them,
or a UW person to broker transfers. Plan for this early if your data lives at CSU or NCAR.
:::

### The free tier

Each researcher's baseline allocation:

- **100,000 CPU core-hours per year**
- **20,000 GPU-hours per year**

That is plenty for getting started — 100,000 core-hours is roughly one 96-core node running
flat out for six weeks. Larger allocations and investor projects exist beyond this.
Core-hours are counted as (cores × wall-clock hours), a reason not to over-ask for resources
(@sec-resources).

### The practical checklist

1. Email **Virginia Iglesias** (<virginia@innosphere.org>) to request a MedicineBow account,
   mentioning that you're an ASCEND/ARID performer.
2. You'll be added to the project and issued a UW username. Your first login is
   @sec-first-login.
3. If you're an external (non-UW) collaborator, say so — you'll get an **ARCC-Only** account,
   which can't use Globus (@sec-moving-data), so ask how you'll move data.

No VPN is required to reach ARCC, on campus or off, so once your account exists you can log
in from anywhere.

## First login, the portal, and SSH keys {#sec-first-login}

### Two ways in: portal and SSH

MedicineBow has a single hostname that serves both the web portal and SSH:
`medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu`.

- **The web portal** (Open OnDemand) is a browser interface: a file explorer, a terminal,
  job submission forms, and interactive apps (desktop sessions, RStudio, Jupyter). Start
  here on day one.
- **SSH** is the terminal way in, and how you'll work day-to-day once set up. It requires a
  key you generate through the portal first.

::: {.callout-note}
## Don't use "Southpass"
Older notes may point you at `southpass.arcc.uwyo.edu`, the portal for the *retired
Beartooth cluster*. The DNS name still resolves but has no live service behind it. The
current portal is `medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu`.
:::

### Step 1 — Log into the portal

Go to <https://medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu> and sign in with your UW username and password.
You'll be prompted for **Duo** two-factor authentication. If you've never set up Duo, do it
at <https://wyosecure.uwyo.edu>. No VPN is needed.

Once in, note the **Files** menu (browse `/home`, `/project`, `/gscratch`), the **Clusters →
Shell** option (a terminal in your browser), and the **Interactive Apps** menu.

### Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager

SSH on MedicineBow is **key-and-certificate based, not password based**. Generate a key pair
through the portal:

1. In the portal, open the **SSH Key Manager**.
2. Generate a key. It downloads as a zip named after your username.
3. Unpack it into your local `~/.ssh` and fix permissions:

```bash
unzip ~/Downloads/<username>.zip -d ~/.ssh
chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh
ssh-add
```

Now you can connect from your own terminal:

```bash
ssh <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu
```

::: {.callout-important}
## SSH keys expire after one year
Roughly a year after setup, your `ssh` stops working — permission denied, no obvious
reason. The key expired. Go back to the portal's SSH Key Manager, generate a fresh key, and
unzip it into `~/.ssh` again. This is by design.
:::

### Step 3 — A comfortable SSH config (optional)

Add this to `~/.ssh/config` on your laptop so you can just type `ssh medbow`:

```
Host medbow
    HostName medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu
    User <username>
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 5
```

`ServerAliveInterval` sends a small keepalive every 60 seconds so campus/VPN firewalls
don't silently drop your connection while you're reading output.

### Which door should I use?

| You want to… | Use |
|---|---|
| First-time setup, generate SSH keys | Portal (required) |
| A quick browser terminal from any machine | Portal → Clusters → Shell |
| A graphical desktop, RStudio, Jupyter | Portal → Interactive Apps |
| Everyday scripting, editing, job submission | SSH from your terminal |
| Drag-and-drop a few files | Portal → Files (for big data, see @sec-moving-data) |

Once you can log in and get a shell prompt, continue to the Linux survival kit (@sec-linux),
or skip ahead to storage (@sec-storage) and Slurm (@sec-why-scheduler) if you already know a terminal.
